error_modes.label: Deviation from the assigned holding radial

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted bearing pointer cross-check after the outbound turn, did not track the assigned holding radial inbound to the fix. The displacement grew beyond 8 degrees from the assigned course and the pattern was flown outside the holding side of the fix. IP intervention was required to re-intercept the inbound course before fix passage, so the deviation from the holding pattern exceeded the maneuver tolerance.
texts.1: SP, due to a rolled-out heading taken without reference to the drift already observed outbound, allowed the inbound course displacement to reach the 8 degree limit of the tolerance. SP did not identify the divergence on the bearing pointer and re-intercepted the assigned radial only after verbal prompting by the IP, with most of the inbound leg already flown. The pattern was recovered inside the limit without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to an imprecise roll-out from the turn onto the inbound leg, displaced the aircraft between 5 and 8 degrees from the assigned holding radial. SP detected the displacement on the bearing pointer during the cross-check and re-intercepted the course early on the inbound leg without IP intervention. The deviation from the holding pattern remained inside the outer tolerance band for the rest of the circuit.
texts.3: SP tracked the assigned holding radial within 5 degrees throughout the entry and every subsequent circuit. Course corrections were small, applied on the bearing pointer indication before the displacement developed, and held through each turn. The inbound leg was flown established on the assigned course on every pass over the fix.
texts.4: SP held the assigned holding radial with negligible displacement on every circuit, the roll-out headings requiring no measurable correction inbound. The bearing pointer was kept centered from turn completion to fix passage and the pattern was reproduced identically on each lap.
texts.marginal: SP remained inside the radial tolerance, but the pattern was consistently displaced to the same side of the assigned course and the correction was repeated on each circuit instead of being fixed once. The trend is a drift correction angle established too late in the inbound leg. SP is expected to set the correction angle on the first circuit and keep the inbound course centered thereafter.

texts_at.0: SP tracked the assigned holding radial with the IP flying the first inbound intercept and talking through the bearing pointer cross-check after each outbound turn. This is SP's first exposure to holding pattern tracking, and cross-checking the bearing pointer immediately after the turn has not yet become a habit. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin cross-checking the bearing pointer independently after each turn, with the IP available to confirm the picture.
texts_at.1: SP tracked the assigned holding radial to the standard expected at this stage, letting the inbound displacement reach the 8 degree limit of the tolerance before it was re-intercepted. The re-intercept followed verbal prompting by the IP rather than SP's own cross-check of the bearing pointer. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to identify the divergence on the bearing pointer during the cross-check rather than only after it is called.
texts_at.2: SP detected the displacement on the bearing pointer without IP intervention, letting it reach about 6 degrees off the assigned holding radial before re-intercepting the course early on the inbound leg. The displacement is still consistently to the same side of the assigned course, from a correction angle set late in the outbound leg. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set the correction angle on the first circuit so the displacement stops repeating to the same side.
texts_at.3: SP tracked the assigned holding radial within 5 degrees on most circuits, with course corrections small and applied on the bearing pointer indication before the displacement developed. One inbound leg needed a slightly larger correction following a stronger than usual crosswind, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold the same margin on that leg as on the rest of the pattern.

texts_above.1: SP tracked the assigned holding radial, letting the inbound displacement reach about 8 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before it was re-intercepted. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP detected the displacement on the bearing pointer without IP intervention, letting it reach between 5 and 8 degrees from the assigned holding radial before re-intercepting the course early on the inbound leg. Setting the correction angle on the first circuit, rather than repeating the same displacement, would keep the margin steadier. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good radial-tracking discipline.
texts_above.3: SP tracked the assigned holding radial within 5 degrees throughout the entry and every subsequent circuit, with course corrections small and applied on the bearing pointer indication before the displacement developed, holding through each turn. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good pattern discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held the assigned holding radial with negligible displacement on every circuit, with the roll-out headings requiring no measurable correction inbound and the bearing pointer kept centered from turn completion to fix passage. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent radial precision.

error_modes.label: Airspeed control in the holding pattern

texts.0: SP, due to a power setting left unadjusted when the aircraft was leveled at the holding altitude, did not stabilize the aircraft at holding airspeed. The airspeed deviation exceeded 20 knots and persisted through the turn, so the pattern was flown at a speed for which the leg timing and the protected airspace were not valid. IP intervention on the power lever was required to return the aircraft to holding airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan that remained on the bearing pointer while power was left at the descent setting, allowed the airspeed to reach the 20 knot limit of the tolerance. SP did not detect the trend on the airspeed indicator and reset the power only after the IP called the deviation, by which time the outbound leg was complete. The airspeed was recovered inside the limit without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to a power correction made in one step without allowance for the trim change, let the airspeed deviate between 10 and 20 knots from the holding airspeed during the turns. SP identified the deviation on the airspeed indicator and reset power and trim early enough to be stabilized before the next fix passage, without IP intervention. Holding airspeed was maintained inside the outer tolerance band for the remainder of the pattern.
texts.3: SP stabilized the aircraft at holding airspeed within 10 knots and held it through entry, both turns and both legs. Power was set once for the configuration and trimmed off, with small corrections applied as soon as the trend appeared on the airspeed indicator. Speed control did not vary measurably between the outbound and inbound legs.
texts.4: SP held holding airspeed with negligible variation throughout the pattern, the power setting requiring no correction other than the anticipated allowance for the turns. The aircraft was trimmed hands-off at the holding speed and the indication remained steady across every circuit.
texts.marginal: SP kept the airspeed inside the tolerance, but the speed was consistently held above the planned holding value and each turn produced a further increase that had to be corrected. The trend is a power setting chased after the fact rather than anticipated at roll-in. SP is expected to set and trim the holding power setting on the first leg and lead the correction into each turn.

texts_at.0: SP flew the pattern with the IP setting holding power at level-off and talking through the airspeed indicator scan through each turn. This is SP's first exposure to holding airspeed control, and scanning the airspeed indicator through the descent-to-holding transition has not yet been built. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin scanning the airspeed indicator independently at level-off, with the IP available to call any trend that is missed.
texts_at.1: SP held holding airspeed to the standard expected at this stage, letting the deviation reach the 20 knot limit of the tolerance before power was reset. The reset followed the IP calling the deviation rather than SP's own scan of the airspeed indicator. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to bring the airspeed indicator into the scan as power is set at level-off rather than after the descent setting has already caused a trend.
texts_at.2: SP identified the deviation on the airspeed indicator without IP intervention, letting it grow to around 15 knots off the holding airspeed during the turns before resetting power and trim early. The power correction is still made in one step without allowance for the trim change. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to make the power correction together with the trim adjustment rather than one after the other.
texts_at.3: SP stabilized the aircraft at holding airspeed within 10 knots and held it through entry, both turns and both legs, on most of the pattern, with power set once and small corrections applied as soon as the trend appeared. One turn needed a slightly larger correction than the rest, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold that turn to the same margin as the others.

texts_above.1: SP held holding airspeed, letting the deviation reach about 20 knots, at the tolerance limit, before power was reset. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified the deviation on the airspeed indicator without IP intervention, letting it reach between 10 and 20 knots from the holding airspeed during the turns before resetting power and trim early. Making the power correction together with the trim adjustment, rather than one after the other, would keep that deviation smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound power-and-trim coordination.
texts_above.3: SP stabilized the aircraft at holding airspeed within 10 knots and held it through entry, both turns and both legs, with power set once for the configuration and trimmed off and small corrections applied as soon as the trend appeared on the airspeed indicator. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed airspeed control.
texts_above.4: SP held holding airspeed with negligible variation throughout the pattern, the power setting requiring no correction other than the anticipated allowance for the turns, with the aircraft trimmed hands-off at the holding speed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional airspeed stability.

error_modes.label: Estimated time over the IAF and leg timing accuracy

texts.0: SP, due to leg timing started at the wrong point and never reconciled with the groundspeed, did not produce a usable estimate for the fix. The actual time over the IAF differed from the estimate passed to ATC by more than 2 minutes, so the sequencing information given to the controller was invalid. IP intervention was required to re-time the pattern and pass a corrected estimate.
texts.1: SP, due to an outbound leg timed from the wings-level point on one circuit and from abeam the fix on the next, allowed the error in the estimated time over the IAF to reach the 2 minute limit. SP did not recognize that the legs were inconsistent and revised the estimate only after the IP prompted a recomputation. The corrected estimate was passed inside the limit without further intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to an outbound leg flown without adjustment for the tailwind component, produced an estimated time over the IAF in error by between 1 and 2 minutes. SP recognized the discrepancy after the first fix passage, adjusted the outbound leg timing and passed a revised estimate to ATC without IP intervention. The subsequent estimates remained inside the outer tolerance band.
texts.3: SP computed and passed an estimated time over the IAF accurate to within 1 minute. The outbound leg was timed from the correct reference point and adjusted so that the inbound leg met the required timing on each circuit. The estimate was reviewed against the actual fix passage and confirmed on every lap.
texts.4: SP produced estimated times over the IAF with negligible error on every circuit, the inbound leg timing repeating within a few seconds. The outbound leg was adjusted for the observed wind on the first pass and the estimate required no revision thereafter.
texts.marginal: SP kept the estimated time over the IAF inside the tolerance, but the error was consistently in the same direction and the outbound leg was shortened by a rough allowance instead of a computed one. The trend is a timing correction sized by feel rather than derived from the observed inbound leg. SP is expected to compute the outbound adjustment from the timed inbound leg and hold the estimate stable across circuits.

texts_at.0: SP timed the pattern with the IP computing the outbound leg reference and talking through reconciling the estimate with the observed wind. This is SP's first exposure to timing a holding pattern, and reconciling the outbound leg with a consistent reference point has not yet become routine. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin timing the outbound leg independently from a consistent reference, with the IP available to confirm the estimate.
texts_at.1: SP timed the outbound leg to the standard expected at this stage, letting the estimate error reach the 2 minute limit of the tolerance before it was revised. The revision followed the IP prompting a recomputation rather than SP's own recognition of the inconsistency. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to time the outbound leg from the same reference point on every circuit rather than switching between references.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the discrepancy after the first fix passage without IP intervention, letting the estimate error stand at about 1.5 minutes before adjusting the outbound leg timing and passing a revised estimate. The outbound leg is still flown without adjustment for the tailwind component before the first correction. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to adjust the outbound leg for the observed wind from the first circuit rather than after an inaccurate estimate has already been passed.
texts_at.3: SP computed and passed an estimated time over the IAF accurate to within 1 minute on most circuits, timing the outbound leg from the correct reference point and adjusting so the inbound leg met the required timing. One estimate needed a small revision after review against the actual fix passage, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold that estimate as accurate as the rest of the circuits.

texts_above.1: SP timed the outbound leg, letting the estimate error reach about 2 minutes, at the tolerance limit, before it was revised. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the discrepancy after the first fix passage without IP intervention, letting the estimate error stand between 1 and 2 minutes before adjusting the outbound leg timing and passing a revised estimate. Adjusting the outbound leg for the observed wind from the first circuit, rather than after an inaccurate estimate is passed, would keep that error smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady timing discipline.
texts_above.3: SP computed and passed an estimated time over the IAF accurate to within 1 minute, timing the outbound leg from the correct reference point and adjusting so the inbound leg met the required timing on each circuit, with the estimate reviewed against the actual fix passage. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good timing accuracy.
texts_above.4: SP produced estimated times over the IAF with negligible error on every circuit, the inbound leg timing repeating within a few seconds, with the outbound leg adjusted for the observed wind on the first pass and no revision needed thereafter. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior timing consistency.

error_modes.label: Holding entry sector determination and protected airspace

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the entry sector rules of AFMAN 11-202 VOL3, selected an entry that did not correspond to the inbound course and the holding side. The aircraft was flown outside the protected holding airspace on the initial circuit, with the radial deviation exceeding 8 degrees, and the pattern was not established in accordance with the standardized procedure. IP intervention was required to identify the correct entry and recover the aircraft into the holding airspace.
texts.1: SP, due to an entry sector determined without reference to the inbound course relative to the holding radial, began an entry appropriate to a different sector. SP recognized the error only after the IP described the correct entry and rejoined the pattern late, having flown the first outbound leg on the non-holding side with the radial deviation reaching 8 degrees, at the tolerance limit. The aircraft was returned inside the holding airspace without control intervention by the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to an entry sector decision taken late in the run-in to the fix, flew the initial turn with an imprecise heading for the selected entry and displaced the aircraft toward the edge of the holding airspace, with the radial deviation reaching about 6 degrees, between the desired and the maximum tolerance. SP identified the displacement, corrected the entry heading and established the pattern correctly on the first circuit without IP intervention. The aircraft remained within the holding airspace throughout.
texts.3: SP determined the entry sector before reaching the fix, selected the correct entry for the inbound course and flew it in accordance with the standardized procedure. The aircraft remained on the holding side throughout the entry and the pattern was established on the first circuit. No prompting on entry type or protected airspace was required.
texts.4: SP briefed the entry sector well before the fix, flew the correct entry with negligible heading error and was established in the pattern from the first outbound leg. The aircraft was kept comfortably inside the holding airspace with the geometry of the entry never in doubt.
texts.marginal: SP selected and flew the correct entry and stayed within the holding airspace, but the entry decision was made only in the last seconds before fix passage and the first turn was consequently rushed. The trend is late mental preparation of the entry geometry rather than any error in the rule itself. SP is expected to determine the entry sector during the run-in and fly the first turn without haste.

texts_at.0: SP entered the hold with the IP describing the entry sector and talking through the inbound course relative to the holding radial. This is SP's first exposure to the entry sector rules, and determining the entry from the inbound course has not yet been learned well enough to apply without help. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin determining the entry sector independently from the inbound course, with the IP available to confirm the selection.
texts_at.1: SP selected the entry sector to the standard expected at this stage, with the radial deviation reaching 8 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before the pattern was rejoined. The rejoin followed the IP describing the correct entry rather than SP's own reference to the inbound course. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to determine the entry sector from the inbound course relative to the holding radial before the turn is started, not after it proves wrong.
texts_at.2: SP identified the displacement and corrected the entry heading without IP intervention, with the radial deviation reaching about 6 degrees before the pattern was established correctly. The entry sector decision is still taken late in the run-in to the fix rather than well before it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to make the entry decision earlier in the run-in so the first turn is not flown with an imprecise heading.
texts_at.3: SP determined the entry sector before reaching the fix, selected the correct entry for the inbound course and flew it in accordance with the standardized procedure on most entries, remaining on the holding side within 5 degrees of the holding radial throughout. One entry was decided a little later than the rest, without leaving the holding airspace. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to decide that entry as early as the others.

texts_above.1: SP selected the entry sector, with the radial deviation reaching about 8 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before the pattern was rejoined. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified the displacement and corrected the entry heading without IP intervention, with the radial deviation reaching about 6 degrees before the pattern was established correctly. Making the entry decision earlier in the run-in, rather than late, would keep that displacement smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable entry-sector judgment.
texts_above.3: SP determined the entry sector before reaching the fix, selected the correct entry for the inbound course and flew it in accordance with the standardized procedure, remaining on the holding side throughout the entry with the pattern established on the first circuit. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate entry selection.
texts_above.4: SP briefed the entry sector well before the fix, flew the correct entry with negligible heading error and was established in the pattern from the first outbound leg, kept comfortably inside the holding airspace with the geometry of the entry never in doubt. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary entry planning.

error_modes.label: Wind compensation and correction of the outbound leg

texts.0: SP, due to no drift correction angle applied on either leg, did not compensate for the wind change between circuits. The pattern degraded progressively downwind, with the inbound course intercepted more than 8 degrees off the assigned radial and the leg lengths no longer representative of the pattern. IP intervention was required to reset the drift correction and re-establish the pattern within the standards.
texts.1: SP, due to a drift correction angle carried over from the entry without review, did not compensate for the wind change as the pattern progressed. The resulting displacement reached 8 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before SP revised the correction, only after the IP called the drift, having flown a full circuit with the pattern displaced. The correction was then applied without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to a drift correction angle applied to the inbound leg only, did not initially compensate for the wind on the outbound leg and the pattern was displaced about 6 degrees, within the outer tolerance band. SP recognized the displacement on the second circuit, applied the outbound correction and adjusted the outbound timing without IP intervention. The pattern was restored to the standard shape for the remaining circuits.
texts.3: SP established the drift correction angle from the first inbound leg and applied the appropriate correction outbound, compensating for the wind change without IP intervention. Outbound timing was adjusted so that the inbound leg remained the required length as the wind changed. The pattern held its shape across successive circuits.
texts.4: SP identified the wind on the first circuit and applied a drift correction that kept the pattern geometrically stable with negligible displacement thereafter. Outbound heading and timing were adjusted together as the wind changed, and no circuit required a corrective intercept.
texts.marginal: SP compensated for the wind within the standards, but the correction was rebuilt on every circuit instead of being refined from the previous one and the pattern shape varied between laps. The trend is a drift correction treated as a new problem each time round. SP is expected to carry forward and refine the correction angle so that successive circuits repeat.

texts_at.0: SP flew the pattern with the IP setting the drift correction angle and talking through reviewing it as the wind changed between circuits. This is SP's first exposure to reviewing a drift correction circuit by circuit, and carrying the entry value forward without revising it has not yet been corrected by habit. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin reviewing the drift correction independently at each circuit, with the IP available to confirm the amount.
texts_at.1: SP compensated for wind between circuits to the standard expected at this stage, letting the displacement reach 8 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before the correction was revised. The revision followed the IP calling the drift rather than SP's own review of the entry correction. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to review the drift correction angle at each circuit rather than carrying the entry value forward unchanged.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the displacement on the second circuit without IP intervention, letting the pattern displace about 6 degrees, within the outer tolerance band, before applying the outbound correction and adjusting the timing. The outbound leg is still uncompensated for a circuit after the inbound correction is established. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to apply the outbound correction on the same circuit as the inbound one rather than a circuit later.
texts_at.3: SP established the drift correction angle from the first inbound leg and applied the appropriate correction outbound on most circuits, with the pattern held to 5 degrees off the assigned radial. The wind change was compensated without IP intervention and outbound timing was adjusted so the inbound leg remained the required length. One circuit needed a small refinement after a wind shift, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to refine that circuit's correction as promptly as the rest of the pattern.

texts_above.1: SP compensated for wind between circuits, letting the displacement reach about 8 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before the correction was revised. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the displacement on the second circuit without IP intervention, letting the pattern displace about 6 degrees before applying the outbound correction and adjusting the timing. Applying the outbound correction on the same circuit as the inbound one, rather than a circuit later, would keep that displacement smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured wind-correction sequencing.
texts_above.3: SP established the drift correction angle from the first inbound leg and applied the appropriate correction outbound, compensating for the wind change without IP intervention and adjusting outbound timing so the inbound leg remained the required length as the wind changed, with the pattern holding its shape across circuits. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise drift-angle management.
texts_above.4: SP identified the wind on the first circuit and applied a drift correction that kept the pattern geometrically stable with negligible displacement thereafter, adjusting outbound heading and timing together as the wind changed with no circuit requiring a corrective intercept. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate pattern stability.

error_modes.label: Pre-descent checks and checklist discipline in the hold

texts.0: SP, due to distraction by a secondary cockpit task during a critical phase, did not execute the pre-descent checks while established in holding. The aircraft was taken out of the hold toward the approach with the checklist still incomplete, three required items unverified, and no attempt made to catch up before the descent began. IP intervention was required to stop the descent and have the checklist accomplished.
texts.1: SP, due to attention absorbed by the timing of the outbound leg, omitted two items of the pre-descent checks and did not detect the omission on the flow. SP completed the checklist only after being reminded by the IP, immediately before leaving the hold and with no margin remaining. The checks were finished without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to the pre-descent checks being started late on the inbound leg, ran the checklist under time pressure and initially skipped one item in the flow. SP caught the omission on the challenge and response, completed the checks with about 30 seconds to spare before the holding fix and required no IP intervention. The aircraft left the hold correctly configured.
texts.3: SP executed the pre-descent checks in the hold, complete and in sequence, with time available before leaving the pattern. The checks were run at a point in the circuit that did not compete with the timing and tracking tasks. All items were verified against the indications rather than recited.
texts.4: SP executed the pre-descent checks early in the holding pattern, complete, in sequence and without any interruption to the tracking, timing or airspeed control. Each item was confirmed against the corresponding indication and the aircraft was fully prepared well before the departure from the hold.
texts.marginal: SP completed the pre-descent checks correctly, but they were consistently begun on the last inbound leg and left no reserve if the clearance had come earlier. The trend is checklist timing driven by the clearance rather than planned within the circuit. SP is expected to schedule the checks one circuit earlier so that the departure from the hold is never the limiting factor.

texts_at.0: SP worked the pre-descent checks with the IP calling the flow and talking through completing the checklist with time to spare before leaving the hold. This is SP's first exposure to running the pre-descent checks inside a timed pattern, and scheduling them early in the circuit has not yet been built. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin scheduling the checks independently earlier in the circuit, with the IP available to confirm the flow.
texts_at.1: SP completed the pre-descent checks to the standard expected at this stage, finishing with no margin remaining before leaving the hold after two items had been omitted and caught late on the flow. The completion followed the IP's reminder rather than SP's own detection of the omission. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to detect an omitted item on the flow itself rather than needing a reminder immediately before leaving the hold.
texts_at.2: SP caught the omission on the challenge and response without IP input, completing the checks with about 30 seconds to spare before the holding fix after one item was initially skipped. The checks are still started late on the inbound leg rather than earlier in the circuit. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start the checks earlier in the circuit so they are not run under time pressure.
texts_at.3: SP executed the pre-descent checks in the hold, complete and in sequence, with about 1 minute in hand before leaving the pattern on most circuits, verifying each item against the indications rather than reciting it. One circuit had the checks run with a slightly narrower margin, without an item being missed. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to build the same margin into that circuit as into the rest of the pattern.

texts_above.1: SP completed the pre-descent checks, finishing with no margin remaining before leaving the hold, at the tolerance limit, after two items had been caught late on the flow. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP caught the omission on the challenge and response without IP input, completing the checks with about 30 seconds to spare before the holding fix after one item was initially skipped. Starting the checks earlier in the circuit, rather than late on the inbound leg, would keep that margin wider. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid checklist recovery.
texts_above.3: SP executed the pre-descent checks in the hold, complete and in sequence, with time available before leaving the pattern, run at a point in the circuit that did not compete with the timing and tracking tasks and every item verified against the indications. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed checklist timing.
texts_above.4: SP executed the pre-descent checks early in the holding pattern, complete, in sequence and without any interruption to the tracking, timing or airspeed control, confirming each item against the corresponding indication well before the departure from the hold. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior checklist discipline.

error_modes.label: Compliance with ATC holding instructions and readback

texts.0: SP, due to a readback made in non-standard phraseology that the controller did not challenge, accepted holding instructions that differed from those issued. The aircraft was held on the wrong side of the fix, with the leg length flown more than 2 minutes off the cleared value, and the expect further clearance time was not observed, so the clearance was not complied with. IP intervention was required to query ATC and correct the holding instructions.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete readback that omitted the holding side and the leg length, did not comply with part of the ATC instruction and did not detect the discrepancy from the controller's response. The leg length flown reached 2 minutes off the cleared value, at the tolerance limit, before SP corrected the pattern, only after the IP prompted a verification with ATC, having already flown a circuit against the clearance. Compliance was restored without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to a readback that reordered the elements of the holding clearance, initially set the pattern with the leg length about 1.5 minutes off the cleared value, between the tolerances, while the fix, radial and altitude were correct. SP identified the discrepancy on reviewing the clearance, requested confirmation from ATC and corrected the leg length within the first circuit without IP intervention. The remainder of the clearance was complied with throughout.
texts.3: SP read back the holding clearance complete and in standard phraseology, including fix, radial, direction, leg length, altitude and expect further clearance time. The pattern flown matched the clearance issued and all subsequent ATC instructions were complied with promptly. No clarification from the IP was required.
texts.4: SP read back every element of the holding clearance in standard phraseology on first transmission and flew the pattern exactly as cleared. Subsequent ATC instructions were acknowledged and complied with immediately, with the expect further clearance time noted and used in the fuel and approach planning.
texts.marginal: SP complied with the ATC holding instructions and the readbacks were correct, but they were transmitted at a rate that required the controller to confirm elements more than once. The trend is compressed phraseology under workload rather than any misunderstanding of the clearance. SP is expected to keep the readback rate steady so that the first transmission is sufficient.

texts_at.0: SP worked ATC holding instructions with the IP confirming each element of the readback and talking through the standard phraseology and sequence. This is SP's first exposure to reading back a full holding clearance in standard phraseology, and including every element in the right order has not yet become routine. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage.
